en.title: Dan Houser Reveals Bully's Troubled Development and Why Bully 2 Never Happened
en.summary: Former Rockstar VP Dan Houser sheds light on the intense challenges faced during the creation of the beloved 2006 title, **Bully**. He also explains the primary reason **Bully 2** never saw the light of day, a topic that has long intrigued fans.
en.body:
The vibrant, chaotic halls of Bullworth Academy might seem like a natural fit for Rockstar Games, but bringing **Bully** to life was anything but smooth sailing. In a recent interview, former Rockstar VP and writer **Dan Houser** confessed that the development of the 2006 cult classic was a constant struggle, fraught with uncertainty.

> "The development was hard. The game was in trouble all of the time. It was difficult. It was an out-there concept. We were struggling with it. I wasn't sure it was going to be any good. We really wanted it to come together. It was really fun afterwards because it came together really well. The team did a great job. It was a sort of really strong game at the end. It kind of came together very late." — Dan Houser

Launching just over a year after the expansive **Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas**, **Bully** presented a unique challenge as a new intellectual property. Houser highlighted that the game's unconventional premise and the surrounding controversy, fueled by misunderstandings before its release, meant it struggled to gain the necessary attention and distribution support. The team was reportedly so preoccupied with mitigating potential protests and ensuring retailers stocked the game that its creative vision almost faltered.

## The Unfulfilled Promise of Bully 2

For years, fans have clamored for a sequel to the critically acclaimed **Bully**, and **Dan Houser** has now offered a clear explanation for why it never materialized. He primarily cited "bandwidth issues" as the main culprit, a term that suggests Rockstar's internal resources and focus were stretched too thin across its many ambitious projects. While some story elements for **Bully 2** were reportedly conceived, the studio's capacity to pursue it alongside other major titles like **Grand Theft Auto** and **Red Dead Redemption** proved to be the insurmountable obstacle.

> "I think it was just bandwidth issues. You know, if you’ve got a small lead creative team, you can only do so many things." — Dan Houser

This explanation aligns with previous statements, indicating that the decision was less about a lack of creative desire and more about the practical realities of game development at a studio of Rockstar's scale. The sheer ambition and scope of their flagship franchises consistently demanded the lion's share of their attention and resources, leaving little room for other passion projects, no matter how beloved.

## A Community's Lingering Hope

The revelation about **Bully 2**'s shelving, while disappointing, is a familiar narrative for many long-time Rockstar fans. The studio is known for its meticulous approach to game development, often prioritizing quality and polish over rapid release schedules. The fact that **Bully** itself overcame such significant development hurdles to become a lasting favorite speaks volumes about the dedication of the team involved. The community's continued passion for the original game, evidenced by ongoing fan projects and discussions, underscores the potential a sequel could have had, keeping the dream of returning to Bullworth Academy alive for many.

## What's Next

While **Bully 2** remains a shelved project, **Dan Houser**'s reflections offer a valuable insight into Rockstar's development history. Fans can look forward to **Rockstar Games**' upcoming releases, with the highly anticipated **Grand Theft Auto 6** expected to dominate headlines in the near future. Details regarding any potential future revisit to the **Bully** IP have not yet been announced.

content_raw: Rockstar is gearing up for the launch of GTA 6, but, of course, Grand Theft Auto isn’t the only series the developer is known for. Alongside the likes of the beloved Red Dead Redemption games, there are many fans of another open-world adventure from the studio: Bully. Released in 2006 and originally known in Europe as Canis Canem Edit, Bully tells the story of unruly student Jimmy Hopkins getting in and out of trouble during a year at Bullworth Academy. A smaller-scale, less X-rated version of GTA, it launched to critical acclaim. But the road towards launch was far from easy. “The development was hard,” former Rockstar VP and writer of Bully, Dan Houser, said in a new interview as part of our IGN30 Icons Series. “The game was in trouble all of the time. It was difficult. It was an out-there concept. We were struggling with it. I wasn't sure it was going to be any good. We really wanted it to come together. It was really fun afterwards because it came together really well. The team did a great job. It was a sort of really strong game at the end. It kind of came together very late.” Houser went on to explain why the development of Bully proved such a challenge, coming as it did just over a year after GTA: San Andreas. “New IP is very stressful because you're doing something that no one's ever done before,” he said. “And particularly that game, there was all of this controversy around it to do with the name, or people misunderstood it when they'd never seen it. So I think one of the challenges with that game was it never got the attention it deserved. We were too focused on trying to at least get people to stock it or to not protest it before it even came out.” The mid-2000s was an era when controversy followed Rockstar games whenever one was about to hit store shelves, whether it be the snuff-film-fuelled ultraviolence of Manhunt, or the sex minigame mod, Hot Coffee, uncovered in the code of San Andreas. Bully was no different, with some members of the public worried about how its explicit content would translate into a school setting. “There was huge hysteria around it,” Houser stated. “We had to spend most of 2006 diffusing it, so we couldn't positively promote the game in the way we normally would've done. I think that didn't help it. I mean, that was the same time as Hot Coffee, and it felt like things were imploding. It was very stressful. And just go to work each day, wonder who's protesting you that day, and hope that things can shake out properly. I wasn't directly involved. Luckily, I was just sort of right off to the side, and wasn't directly involved in organizing most of that stuff. But it was really stressful for the people involved.” But it wasn’t just external pressures that made the development of Bully difficult. Rockstar also had to wrestle with how to make its style of open-world action-adventure work from the perspective of a teenager.
